capture.final_message:
Treat `Min.min` on filters as `⊓`. The key mechanism is the witness-based definition of `FiniteAtFilter`: a finite-measure set belonging to one filter also belongs to its infimum with any other filter, since `f ⊓ g ≤ f` (remember filter order reverses set inclusion).

Organize the argument around two facts:

1. Prove the general transfer principle
   \[
   \mathrm{FiniteAtFilter}(\mu,f)\;\Rightarrow\;
   \mathrm{FiniteAtFilter}(\mu,f\sqcap g).
   \]
   This gives the first conjunct, and—using the other projection `f ⊓ g ≤ g`, or `inf_comm`—shows that the left side of the displayed `Iff` is always true.

2. Characterize the measure-cofinite filter:
   \[
   \mu.\mathrm{cofinite}=\bot
   \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   \mu(\mathrm{univ})<\infty
   \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   \mathrm{IsFiniteMeasure}\,\mu.
   \]
   For the forward direction, test membership of `∅`; belonging to `μ.cofinite` means its complement `univ` has finite measure. Conversely, if `μ univ` is finite, every complement has finite measure, so every set belongs to `μ.cofinite`, making it `⊥`.

Thus both propositions inside the `Iff` hold universally, so conclude the equivalence by proving each independently. The only subtlety is the reversed order convention for filters.
